issues.legal_issue: A child born during a valid marriage is presumed to be the husband’s legitimate child unless non-access at any time when the child could have been conceived is proved.
material_facts: The child was born while his mother’s valid marriage to the deceased was continuing.
The deceased denied paternity, but the mother testified that the child was his and that she had not left the marital home.

The mother lived at her father’s house about a furlong from the deceased’s home, and the evidence did not establish that the spouses had no access to each other when the child could have been conceived.
issues.conclusion: The presumption of legitimacy was not rebutted, and the concurrent finding that the child was the deceased’s legitimate son was left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 makes birth during the continuance of a valid marriage conclusive proof of legitimacy, rebuttable only by proof that the spouses had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten. The court relied on no earlier case on this issue.

rule.if: inheritance_claim_by_child and child_born_during_valid_marriage and not nonaccess_proven

predicates.inheritance_claim_by_child: A child claims an inheritance while another party disputes that the deceased was the child’s parent.
predicates.child_born_during_valid_marriage: The child was born while the mother’s valid marriage to the alleged father was continuing.
predicates.nonaccess_proven: Evidence establishes that the spouses had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been conceived.

issues.definition: When a child claims an inheritance, was born during a valid marriage, and non-access at the possible time of conception is not proved, the child’s legitimacy is presumed.

issues.legal_issue: A husband cannot gift ancestral immovable property belonging to a joint family to his wife merely out of affection.
material_facts: The husband executed a gift of immovable joint family property in favour of his second wife.
The gift deed referred to affection, and the donee argued that the gift covered only a reasonable portion of the property.
The property was ancestral immovable property.
issues.conclusion: The gift to the wife was invalid; affection did not make a gift of ancestral immovable property permissible.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a Hindu father or other managing member may make a gift of ancestral immovable property within reasonable limits for pious purposes, but affection does not make a gift of such property to a wife permissible. The court relied on Kamala Devi v. Bachu Lal Gupta, [1957] S.C.R. 452, and Guramma Bharatar Chanbassappa Deshmukh v. Malappa, [1964] 4 S.C.R. 497, for the limited scope of gifts for pious purposes and declined to extend that scope to gifts to a wife.

rule.if: challenge_to_property_gift and property_is_ancestral_immovable and husband_gifted_to_wife and gift_based_on_affection

predicates.challenge_to_property_gift: A civil proceeding challenges the validity of a gift of property.
predicates.property_is_ancestral_immovable: The gifted property is ancestral immovable property belonging to a joint family.
predicates.husband_gifted_to_wife: A husband made the gift to his wife.
predicates.gift_based_on_affection: The gift was defended as having been made out of affection.

issues.definition: If a challenged gift concerns ancestral immovable joint family property, was made by a husband to his wife, and rests on affection, the gift is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A purported obligation to carry out a father’s marriage-time promise cannot validate a husband’s gift of ancestral immovable property to his wife, and the gift cannot be validated as a gift to a daughter-in-law for her separate property.
material_facts: The gift deed stated that the husband was acting in accordance with a promise made by his father at the time of the wife’s marriage and the father’s directions to make provision for her.
The gift was of ancestral immovable property from the husband to his wife, who was his father’s daughter-in-law.
The donee argued that the gift should be upheld as fulfilling a pious obligation and that gifts to a daughter-in-law could become her separate property.
issues.conclusion: The father’s alleged promise and directions did not make the gift valid; neither a pious obligation nor the rules concerning gifts to a daughter-in-law’s separate property permitted a gift of ancestral immovable property in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Hindu law permits reasonable gifts of ancestral immovable property for pious purposes, including reasonable provision for a daughter in the circumstances recognized in Kamala Devi v. Bachu Lal Gupta, [1957] S.C.R. 452, and Guramma Bharatar Chanbassappa Deshmukh v. Malappa, [1964] 4 S.C.R. 497. That principle does not extend to a father-in-law’s gift of ancestral immovable property to a daughter-in-law, or to a son’s purported discharge of an obligation to make such a gift. Rules permitting gifts to a daughter-in-law that become her separate property do not authorize gifts of ancestral immovable property.

rule.if: challenge_to_property_gift and property_is_ancestral_immovable and husband_gifted_to_wife and gift_purportedly_fulfills_fathers_marriage_promise

predicates.challenge_to_property_gift: A civil proceeding challenges the validity of a gift of property.
predicates.property_is_ancestral_immovable: The gifted property is ancestral immovable property belonging to a joint family.
predicates.husband_gifted_to_wife: A husband made the gift to his wife.
predicates.gift_purportedly_fulfills_fathers_marria: The gift was said to fulfill the husband’s father’s promise or directions made in connection with the wife’s marriage.

issues.definition: If a challenged gift of ancestral immovable joint family property from a husband to his wife is said to fulfill his father’s marriage-time promise, the gift is invalid.
